newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARIAN AUTO FIRM RABA UPS PROFITS, GLOBALISES.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARIAN AUTO FIRM RABA UPS PROFITS, GLOBALISES.

text.p: Hungarian auto company Raba Rt, which is slated for privatisation next year, expects its fifth consecutive year of profits in 1996 on the strength of an accelerating globalisation drive.

"In 1996, Raba will achieve over 27 billion forints in turnover and one billion forints in pre-tax profits," Barnabas Zalan, Raba's general manager, said at an event celebrating the company's 100th year of operation in Gyor in western Hungary.
"Raba's production capacity now meets international standards, and its financial position is increasingly strong."

The company, whose full name is Raba Magyar Vagon -es Gepgyar Rt, posted a pre-tax profit of 700 million forints on 23.7 billion forints in revenue in 1995 and a pre-tax profit of 547 million forints on 20.3 billion forints in revenue in 1994.

Raba, a supplier of major parts for the bus and truck industy, already claims to be Hungary's top exporter to the United States. Recently it started sales to Japan and Korea, while projects in China and Russia are underway.

"Our main goal is to expand our presence in markets throughout the world," Kalman Kozma, Raba's deputy director for axle sales, told Reuters. "We are flexible, and we have been working hard to identify and develop products for a growing number of customers."
Raba's success revolves increasingly around axles and axle parts -- generating roughly 70 percent of the company's revenue -- and sales will continue to grow, Kozma said.

Its U.S. sales will rise from $55 million in 1989 to an expected $90 million in 1996 and $100 million in 1997, he said. Asian sales also will grow, spurting to $5 million next year from $1 million this year in Korea; and to several million dollars in 1997 from $500,000 in 1996 in Japan, he added.
Raba dates its international experience to 1899, when it started exporting railway cars to Africa and western Europe. It also shipped carriages for London's first underground train.
Though Hungary's subjection to communism for 40 years stunted Raba's development, the company has recovered quickly.

Since the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, Raba has formed joint ventures with German axle maker Bergische Achsenfabrik Fr Kotz und Soehne, U.S. engine manufacturer Detroit Diesel Corp and U.S. automaker General Motors Corp .

Raba's multinational clients now include the world's three largest axle manufacturers -- Dana Corp , Eaton Corp and Rockwell International Corp of the U.S. Raba also supplies Swedish automaker AB Volvo and U.S. agricultural and construction vehicle maker Case Corp.

This year, Raba also started delivering axles to several Asian conglomerates that build vehicles, including Daewoo Group, Hyundai Group and Ssangyong Group of Korea; and Isuzu Motors Ltd and Nissan Motor Co Ltd of Japan.
"Raba is a major player in eastern Europe," Eric Gibbins, editor of newsletter Truck and Bus Builder, said. "It's not as sophisticated as Eaton and Rockwell, but it's not far behind."
Its privatisation has attracted several potential investors, including clients Daewoo, Czech conglomerate Skoda AS and U.S. truck company Marmon Group Inc.

Raba needs outside investors to continue bolstering its market base and its products, and some company officials said Skoda is the best suitor because the Czech company could help Raba develop its business in former communist Europe.
But Raba also is wary of a client acquiring its shares, fearing that such an investor will jeopardise other business.

"If a company like Daewoo buys us, we could lose contracts from other Korean automakers -- and possibly from European and Japanese automakers," a Raba official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters. "We want an investor that will bring new business to us -- not threaten our existing business."
The Hungarian government, which owns nearly 92 percent of Raba, consequently might start the privatisation by selling a small stake to a non-automotive company in early 1997, he said.
Around 25 percent of Raba's shares could float on the Budapest Stock Exchange in 1998, and 20 percent of the equity would be reserved for Raba's managers and workers, he added.
"Currently, we have to seek financial and strategic investors who are interested in a minority stake in Raba -- between five percent and 20 percent," the official said.
